title: Building trustworthy AI by fencing it in, not predicting it
text: In October this year, OpenAI disclosed that two of its AI agents had switched off the systems built to monitor them. One muted its own safety alerts after misreading an instruction not to send messages; the other removed its monitoring integration during migration, then said it hadn’t. title: Surveillance Isn't Safety: A Comic About Organizing Against Flock and Other Foes
text:
In the new comic "Surveillance Isn't Safety"—available for free today— cartoonist Bryn Adams explores the growing movement against mass surveillance through their involvement in the community fight against Flock Safety in Cleveland, Ohio. It's a personal journey that will resonate widely with residents in hundreds of cities where communities are drawing the line against automated license plate readers (ALPRs). 

Jump to the Comic

Or download the PDF

Published in collaboration between EFF and Crucial Comix, Bryn's comic captures the authenticity of the grassroot backlash against the surveillance industry—undercutting Flock founder Garrett Langley's latest dubious defense that public opposition of his company's product isn't real.

At the International Association of Chiefs of Police conference this fall, Langley accused the anti-surveillance activism of being driven by Russian bots and as being "inorganic." He pointed to the fact that many local groups were using similar language in their protest signs as supposed proof, when in reality, shared slogans are one of the hallmarks of a social movement. This was all misdirection from the grim realities that Flock and other ALPR systems facilitate: the mistakes are real; the abuse is real; the racism is real; and the targeting of dissenters, migrants, and abortion seekers is real. And, importantly, the cancelled contracts are real. 

Bryn's comic sheds light on the real abuses and threats driving communities to mobilize against Flock, Axon, and other ALPR vendors. It shows that coast-to-coast activism doesn't happen overnight—any more than a comic appears out of thin air as a finished product. As advisors on the cartoon, EFF watched how Bryn's script evolved from rough sketches to penciled drawings, then to inked and shaded panels, mirroring how the long-running movement against mass surveillance has steadily snowballed over the last few years. 

There is nothing “inorganic” about either: Both are built on passion, commitment, and putting in the work. 

Surveillance Isn't Safety

Joining the fight against Flock and other foes

Author: Bryn Adams, Editors: Shay Mirk (Crucial Comix) and Dave Maass (EFF)

This comic is jointly published by Crucial Comix and the Electronic Frontier Foundation.  This comic is published under a Creative Commons Noncommercial license. You are free to share or republish this comic for noncommercial purposes as long as you credit Bryn Adams as the creator. 

Download a PDF version of the comic here.  A text file including the dialogue and descriptions is available here. 

Bryn Adams is a writer, cartoonist, and illustrator based in Cleveland, Ohio. They have a BA in Environmental Studies from the University of Chicago and a Master of Fine Arts degree from the Center for Cartoon Studies. Their work has appeared in Seven Days, Cleveland Scene Magazine, the Ohio City-Tremont Observer, Crucial Comix, and Jacobin.

title: Voters Reject ALPRs and Surveillance Tech at the Ballot Box
text:
Do automated license plate readers (ALPRs) have any place in our communities? That question has been a hot topic in city council meetings, community conversations, and news coverage around the country for months. This past election day, a couple of U.S communities took it further: to the ballot. 

And overwhelmingly, voters decided that, no, these devices should not be deployed on our streets. We agree! 

In Maine, the coastal community of York voted to remove the town’s existing ALPR cameras and require that any future proposed installations receive voter approval before proceeding. The local initiative ended up on the ballot after constituents gathered enough signatures on a citizens’ petition for a local ordinance. On Election Day, nearly three-quarters of York voters supported the ban. 

Thousands of miles away, voters in League City, Texas also voted against allowing the local police department to continue use of ALPR cameras. That vote was formally approved on November 17, which began a 72-hour window to remove the cameras. Since the election, the cameras have been “bagged” or covered to prevent the collection of data.

At least one city also decided to expand protections afforded to their residents when it comes to the use of surveillance technology. In Pflugerville, Texas, Proposition B passed, now requiring that the City Charter be amended to include “protections governing the collection, use, retention, and oversight of data, facial recognition, and surveillance technologies.” It also requires “a responsible artificial intelligence framework.” 

While every municipality has different rules for how to get a local ordinance placed on the ballot, banning use and securing the removal of surveillance tools locally is a powerful way of protecting your community against devices and data collection that goes far beyond your town lines. 

Surveillance is a choice, not a mandate, and our communities have the power to refuse it. EFF has supported local communities around the country over the last few years in advocating against the procurement of surveillance technologies in their cities, counties, and states. These victories at the ballot box and in city councils show that when mass surveillance is presented as a policy choice, not a technical necessity, communities can and do reject it. 

Do you know what surveillance tools are being used by your local police departments? Check out the Atlas of Surveillance to learn more about the tools deployed in your city, and sign up to volunteer if you want to push for more transparency across the country.

title: The Paramount-Warner Brothers Deal Could Usher in Another Age of Lost Media
text:
There are all sorts of reasons to be against the merger of Paramount and Warner Brothers-Discovery. There's the obvious problem of increasing concentration in the already pretty-concentrated film and TV industry. People have problems with Paramount's owner Skydance interfering  with its news coverage and late night comedy. But one of the biggest is the way we are losing choice and access to information and culture.  

In the context of the digital world, there are two major problems with these mega mergers. One, as we've said in the past, is that it further degrades the already awful state of mainstream streaming services. In short, by increasing the amount of legacy content under their control, major studios don't have to invest in either new content or well-engineered services to get users. Plus, they can pool the data they have on users together in an increasing assault on consumer privacy. A monthly subscription and more information about your habits and interests? Win-win for them.  

Another problem is the disappearing of content. In the digital era, there should be no more lost media. Making and storing copies of media is easier and cheaper than it ever has been. The idea of the persistence of content online has become the adage "the internet never forgets."  

However, since more and more media is locked behind subscription services under the control of fewer and fewer companies—and as physical copies, or even just digital copies that are actually owned by consumers also vanish—access to our common culture is at risk. Incentives to take information and media offline should raise huge red flags. Unfortunately, they are multiplying. 

First, there's the impulse of merged companies to offset the cost of their merger by shelving projects and claiming them as tax write-offs. We saw this the last time Warner Brothers was taken over, with projects being ended in order to take advantage of a specific kind of tax benefit. It has little to do with the quality or even how much or how complete a project is—money is the driving factor and we as a culture are all poorer for it. And we all know it. That's why the outrage eventually led to Coyote vs Acme being released by a much smaller studio. But not every project can count on having the perfect storm that brings a movie or show back from the dead.  

Second, there's the imposition of a new owner's own goals and beliefs upon its new acquisition. Some choices might seem kind of benign, like Discovery axing a lot of family-friendly and kid-oriented content from HBO Max. Of course, when one of the things affected is a pillar of childhood like Sesame Street, the loss of access to old episodes becomes a loss to the culture and not just a change in direction.  

 Another area where we might lose access to information is in the radical shift in direction for news reporting. Reporters have resigned and more are being offered buy-outs to support the change in direction. Whether this will escalate to older projects being removed from streaming services or quietly buried in the recommendation algorithm is yet to be seen, but remains a real possibility. And it's not lost on anyone that one of the outlets reporting on the chaos at CBS News was CNN, which is now owned by the same people who own CBS News. The loss of diverse sources of news, as imperfect as we may have thought they were, hurts all of us. It makes it harder to access information and diverse points of view.  

Finally, media disappears as licenses expire and as studios decide they no longer want to pay residuals or backend deals to the creative people who made the work in the first place. Again, this looks like business decisions but if the works were exclusively available via streaming, those movies disappear forever. That both contributes to the idea that works are disposable and that paying the workers who made the art is not as important as shareholder value. 

On top of all of this, draconian copyright regimes and the anti-user product designs they create have made it nearly impossible for people to archive this material on their own—as many used to using VCRs. It’s easy to see a crisis in access to culture and information brewing, at the same time that it should be easier than ever to preserve and make available our shared digital culture.

title: EFF’s AI Cybersecurity Policy Framework
text:
The news has been filled with stories recently of AI breaching the security of websites. And while it may feel like a new problem because of AI’s involvement, it turns out that there are longstanding existing cybersecurity safety best practices that these companies—some of the largest tech companies in the world—could and should have taken to prevent these breaches.

Recent cybersecurity incidents have shown that some of the world’s largest tech companies have failed to take basic security precautions when testing frontier AI systems on internet-connected systems. Unfortunately, these failures resulted in breaches of numerous third-party websites, including an AI research-sharing platform called Hugging Face and the Australian healthcare system’s website. Even worse, AI developers failed to detect most of the incidents until long after they occurred due to inadequate monitoring of the AI systems during testing. Had the companies abided by basic, common sense security protocols, these incidents likely would not have occurred.

While the White House and some leaders of major AI companies have claimed that no action is necessary, understandably, lawmakers at all levels and of both parties are proposing legislation to create new, additional safety protocols. These incidents may warrant legislative action. However, the good news is that post-incident reports indicate new protocols are largely unnecessary. Following existing best practices would have been enough to prevent the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident and others like it. In other words, responsible AI developers can take immediate action to protect the public by implementing well-established security precautions as they develop and test their systems.

Lawmakers should start by referencing existing legal protections, including claims like negligence, gross negligence, trespass to chattels, Section 1201 of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA), and computer trespass statutes like the Consumer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA) and analogous state law provisions, such as Section 502 of the California Penal Code.

Policymakers can help protect the public by requiring AI developers to follow established security protocols—and creating legal liability for failing to do so. These policies would protect the public from irresponsible actions by AI developers without impeding innovation. To the extent that gaps in existing laws warrant new legislation, EFF recommends the following policy framework:

  • STATUTORY SECURITY REQUIREMENTS: Lawmakers should enact legislation that requires AI developers to adhere to well-established cybersecurity best practices when testing AI systems, such as strong sandboxing and network isolation, least-privilege access, effective logging and monitoring, and clear incident-response procedures
  • REGULATORY STANDARDS: Congress should require an existing federal agency, such as the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)1, to adopt safety standards for pre-deployment development and testing of generative AI systems, based on the established best practices referenced above. The agency should be required to update the standards every 2 years, or earlier as needed due to reported security incidents and/or major technological advancements. These standards should be developed in consultation with academic and nonprofit AI researchers, civil liberties organizations, and commercial AI developers, and adopted through formal agency rulemaking following a notice and comment process. That consultation should include an assessment of potential adverse impacts on competition, with the goal of ensuring that regulatory standards do not effectively lock out potential competitors.
  • LIABILITY: The law should provide for civil liability for AI development and testing that results in unauthorized access to a third party system, if performed under conditions that do not satisfy cybersecurity standards adopted by NIST, or another federal agency responsible for adopting these regulations, unless the company proves it acted reasonably under the circumstances to prevent unauthorized access to third party system 
  • ENFORCEMENT: Both federal and state authorities should be able to hold AI developers accountable where they have failed to meet the minimum standards adopted by the designated federal agency, such as NIST. Providing for state—in addition to federal—enforcement power reduces the risk of regulatory capture. Regulators should require independent investigations and notification of affected parties in the event of a security incident involving unauthorized access to a third party’s computer system. Finally, legislation should include an appropriately targeted private right of action.

The public shouldn’t have to worry about the risks of reckless AI development—or give up the benefits of AI just to prevent irresponsible developers from causing harm. By adopting policies that address demonstrated risks, lawmakers can provide meaningful public protection without hampering the development of useful tools.

1NIST, the NSA, and CISA have recently issued a set of voluntary practices for managing security incidents during the training and evaluation of AI agents. Those practices may inform but do not substitute for the regulatory standards that should be developed according to the public, participatory process outlined here.

title: Amazon Ring’s New Indoor Surveillance Drone Is Not Compatible with Privacy
text:
Amazon Ring has finally announced their long-dreaded indoor drone, a small flying surveillance device connected to their security suite of products that can fly around your house filming and recording things. The device is supposedly designed to fly preset paths across your home and will also activate if a sensor or alarm has been triggered.  

Customers should think twice about purchasing these devices for a number of reasons. These devices are problematic in many of the ways we’ve said Ring’s stationary home surveillance products are a problem, plus some new ways. At a very basic level, they are essentially a window into your house that can be accessed by anyone with access to your account—which has historically included bad actors looking to embarrass or harass Ring users and employees of the company. 

What’s worse, Ring has supercharged the units with its ‘AI Pilot’ to map routes, model the interior of the home, and control movement. This means not only is the footage being sent to corporate servers, but the company is also making inferences about your home to carry out tasks. How much home usage data this is based on, and if it can be used to infer when certain household activities are happening, are both open questions. And presumably, to maintain the preset routes, inferred data about your home will still be held by Ring even after any stored video footage is deleted. 

The risk to your privacy is only compounded once you consider Ring’s renewed partnership with police through the massive surveillance and taser vendor, Axon. Through this partnership, police have the ability to request camera footage from Ring users with just a few clicks on Axon’s platforms. This includes its Fusus platform, an interactive surveillance feed and map police use to manage all the surveillance devices they have access to, like automated license plate readers. It’s unclear exactly what devices police can request footage from, but if this request feature is extended to Ring’s drones, police could easily send requests for footage from inside your house. Sharing is voluntary, but once footage is submitted, it cannot be retracted. Worse still, if your footage is not sitting on Amazon’s servers fully encrypted—and there’s reason to believe their privacy options are not the strongest—police could serve a warrant straight to the company, instead of to you, to get footage from your devices. 

New problems and questions arise because the camera can fly. For instance: if police serve a warrant on Amazon, can they only get the footage from the camera, or could they also get access to control the drone? If the latter, we could be looking at the first full home search in history where police serve a warrant on a third-party tech company and not the resident.  

The CEO of Ring has pitched this product’s safety benefits in several ways, including by saying: “If someone is going around your house at night, and your motion detector goes off on your Ring doorbell, imagine if you see spotlights and something flying across the window...You’re probably not going to go into that house.” But partially justifying a $250 piece of technology that invades your privacy on what an imagined burglar might do doesn’t sound like a foundation for safety—it sounds like security theater and marketing. 

It isn’t new for Ring to prey on the fears and paranoia of people and their properties. This is the latest iteration of that: a patrolling drone or rover wouldn't have been possible even in the world's top museums and art galleries a generation ago. Moving this technology into the household as a common consumer product is another example of companies attempting to lower the bar on surveillance being normalized. 

With previous Ring products, consumers have had to consider what cameras and high-powered microphones can learn about their home usage from the front door. Autonomous flying drones and rovers inside the home add a whole new layer. What can these devices learn about you and your family? And do you really trust that data sitting on a server somewhere? Consumers should consider these risks before subjecting their guests and households to the latest creepy surveillance tool.

title: Honest Brokers in AI Regulation: How Public Comments Introduce Evidence to Regulators
text: The regulation of Artificial Intelligence is susceptible to various forms of capture by industry actors that hold undue influence over the policymaking process, due in part to their information advantage in developing these technologies. In the following paper, we investigate the roles of public commenters in providing evidence to potential regulation in the USA. We build a corpus of 40 potential regulations, and 2,664 public comments submitted by a variety of stakeholders. We computationally process these texts to extract evidence meant to inform regulators, in the form of formal citations and informal references. We find significant differences in the type and amount of evidence supplied: Holding comment length constant, business commenters introduce altogether less evidence, and government, university, and civil society commenters provide significantly more research and legal sources. The publication status of cited research is nearly evenly split, with preprints and peer-reviewed articles being introduced by commenters of all types. We further explore patterns of self-citation and find that while it is prevalent amongst all groups, a small cluster of organizations account for over half of all self-citations in our corpus. Our findings complicate a narrative that public comments alone are means to information capture. We interpret these results in terms of the role that commenters attempt to play in the policymaking process-being either an Issue Advocate or an Honest Broker. These findings on the supply of evidence in public comments shed light on an often overlooked form of policymaking that has implications for how and through what sources information is made accessible to regulators of AI.
